note: Synthetic lessons authored for this experiment. Splits are assigned per lesson before any paraphrase was written. The two seeded demo lessons are added as extra test lessons by the scripts.

sections.t: The Cache-Control header tells browsers and proxies how long a response stays fresh. A max-age of 3600 means the stored copy may be reused for one hour without asking the server.
sections.q: What does max-age in Cache-Control specify?
sections.p: For how long may a browser reuse a stored response before checking with the server?

sections.t: An ETag identifies one version of a resource. The client sends it back in If-None-Match, and the server answers 304 Not Modified when the version is unchanged.
sections.q: What does a 304 Not Modified response mean?
sections.p: When the stored version of a resource is still current, how does the server tell the client?

sections.t: A private directive limits storage to the user's own browser. Shared proxies must not store responses marked private, which protects personalized pages.
sections.q: Why mark a personalized response as private?
sections.p: How do we keep proxies from storing a page that differs for each user?

sections.t: Static assets can carry a content hash in the filename. A changed file gets a new URL, so long-lived caching never serves stale code.
sections.q: How does a content hash in a filename help caching?
sections.p: What lets us cache scripts for a year yet still ship updates immediately?

sections.t: A B-tree index keeps keys in sorted order so the database can find a row in logarithmic time. Without the index the database scans every row in the table.
sections.q: Why is a B-tree lookup faster than a table scan?
sections.p: How can a database find one row without reading the whole table?

sections.t: A composite index on two columns is sorted by the first column, then the second. A query that filters only on the second column cannot use it efficiently.
sections.q: When can a composite index not be used efficiently?
sections.p: If an index covers columns A and B, why does a filter on B alone struggle?

sections.t: A covering index contains every column a query needs. The database answers from the index alone and skips fetching table rows.
sections.q: What is a covering index?
sections.p: Which kind of index lets a query avoid touching the table entirely?

sections.t: EXPLAIN shows the plan the database chose, including scan types and estimated row counts. A large gap between estimated and actual rows suggests stale statistics.
sections.q: What does a gap between estimated and actual rows suggest?
sections.p: How do we spot that the planner is working from outdated statistics?

sections.t: A feature branch isolates work from the main line until it is ready. Reviewers compare the branch against main before it merges.
sections.q: Why develop on a feature branch?
sections.p: How do we keep unfinished work away from the main line?

sections.t: A merge commit joins two histories and preserves both. A rebase replays commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history but new commit hashes.
sections.q: How does a rebase change commit hashes?
sections.p: What is the cost of getting a linear history by replaying commits?

sections.t: A conflict appears when both branches edit the same lines. Edit the file to keep the intended result, stage it, and continue the merge.
sections.q: What causes a merge conflict?
sections.p: When does git stop and ask us to fix files by hand?

sections.t: A tag names one commit permanently, such as v1.2.0. Release builds check out the tag so the shipped code can be rebuilt later.
sections.q: What does a git tag mark?
sections.p: How can we rebuild exactly the code that shipped in a release?

sections.t: A fixed window counts requests in each clock interval and resets at the boundary. A client can send a burst at the end of one window and another at the start of the next.
sections.q: What weakness does a fixed window counter have?
sections.p: How can a client double its allowed traffic around a window boundary?

sections.t: A token bucket refills at a steady rate and each request spends a token. The bucket size sets the largest burst a client may send.
sections.q: What sets the maximum burst in a token bucket?
sections.p: Which parameter limits how many requests can arrive at once?

sections.t: Respond with status 429 when a client exceeds its limit. Include a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients know when to try again.
sections.q: Which status code reports an exceeded rate limit?
sections.p: How does a server tell a client when to retry after throttling it?

sections.t: Limit by authenticated user rather than IP address when possible. Many users can share one address behind a corporate network.
sections.q: Why limit by user instead of IP address?
sections.p: What goes wrong when many people share one network address and we throttle by address?

sections.t: Structure a test in three steps: set up inputs, call the code, and check the result. One clear assertion per behavior makes failures easy to read.
sections.q: What are the three steps of a well-structured test?
sections.p: How should a single test be organized from setup to verification?

sections.t: A stub returns canned data and a mock records how it was called. Replace slow or unreliable dependencies such as the network with doubles.
sections.q: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
sections.p: Which test double verifies how a dependency was called?

sections.t: A flaky test passes and fails without code changes. Common causes are shared state, real clocks, and unordered results.
sections.q: What commonly causes a flaky test?
sections.p: Why might a test pass on one run and fail on the next with the same code?

sections.t: Line coverage reports which lines ran, not whether behavior was verified. A test without assertions can raise coverage while checking nothing.
sections.q: Why can high line coverage be misleading?
sections.p: Does executing a line prove that its behavior was checked?

sections.t: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a read-only layer. Unchanged layers come from the build cache, so order instructions from least to most frequently changed.
sections.q: How should Dockerfile instructions be ordered for caching?
sections.p: What ordering lets a rebuild reuse the most cached layers?

sections.t: A multi-stage build compiles in one image and copies only the artifacts into a small final image. Build tools never reach production.
sections.q: What does a multi-stage build keep out of the final image?
sections.p: How can compilers be used during a build without shipping them?

sections.t: Containers run as root by default. Create an unprivileged user and switch to it so a compromised process has fewer rights.
sections.q: Why switch a container to an unprivileged user?
sections.p: How do we limit what an attacker can do inside a compromised container?

sections.t: The latest tag moves whenever someone pushes. Pin a specific version or digest to get repeatable deployments.
sections.q: Why avoid the latest tag in deployments?
sections.p: What makes a deployment reproducible with respect to its base image?

sections.t: Store a one-way hash of each password rather than the password. A database leak then reveals hashes instead of the passwords themselves.
sections.q: Why store a hash instead of the password?
sections.p: What limits the damage when a user table is leaked?

sections.t: A salt is a random value stored beside each hash and mixed into it. Two users with the same password get different hashes, which defeats precomputed tables.
sections.q: What does a salt prevent?
sections.p: Why do identical passwords produce different stored values?

sections.t: Use a deliberately slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2. The delay is negligible for one login but makes guessing millions of passwords expensive.
sections.q: Why use a deliberately slow hash for passwords?
sections.p: How does bcrypt make offline guessing costly?

sections.t: Return the same message whether the email or the password was wrong. Different messages let an attacker discover which emails have accounts.
sections.q: Why should login errors be identical for wrong email and wrong password?
sections.p: How can error text reveal which accounts exist?

sections.t: Offset pagination skips a number of rows with OFFSET. Deep pages get slower because the database still walks past every skipped row.
sections.q: Why do deep pages get slow with OFFSET?
sections.p: What makes page 5000 more expensive than page 1 when skipping rows?

sections.t: A cursor records the last item seen, such as its id, and the next query asks for rows after it. Pages stay fast and stable while new rows arrive.
sections.q: How does cursor pagination find the next page?
sections.p: What does the client send to continue after the last item it saw?

sections.t: Always sort by a unique column, adding the id as a tie-breaker. Without it, rows with equal values can repeat or vanish between pages.
sections.q: Why add the id as a tie-breaker when sorting?
sections.p: How do we stop duplicate or missing rows across pages?

sections.t: Cap the page size on the server. An unbounded limit parameter lets one request pull the whole table.
sections.q: Why cap page size on the server?
sections.p: What prevents one request from reading an entire table through a limit parameter?

sections.t: Use error for failures that need action and warn for recoverable surprises. Info records normal milestones, and debug is for detail turned on while investigating.
sections.q: When should code log at error level?
sections.p: Which level is for failures that someone must act on?

sections.t: Write logs as JSON objects with named fields. Fields such as requestId can be filtered and counted by a log search tool.
sections.q: Why write logs as JSON objects?
sections.p: How do named fields make logs easier to search?

sections.t: Never log passwords, tokens, or full card numbers. Redact them before they reach the logger because logs are copied to many systems.
sections.q: What must never be written to logs?
sections.p: Why redact secrets before logging instead of cleaning logs later?

sections.t: Attach one request id to every log line a request produces. An engineer can then follow the request across services.
sections.q: What is a request id used for in logs?
sections.p: How can we trace one request through several services?

sections.t: A cron expression has five fields for minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. The expression 0 2 * * * runs at 02:00 every day.
sections.q: What do the five fields of a cron expression represent?
sections.p: How is a daily run at two in the morning written in cron?

sections.t: If a job takes longer than its interval, a second copy can start. Take a lock at the start so the later run exits immediately.
sections.q: How do we stop two copies of a scheduled job overlapping?
sections.p: What happens when a job runs longer than its schedule interval?

sections.t: Cron uses the server time zone unless told otherwise. Daylight saving changes can skip or repeat a local hour, so schedule critical jobs in UTC.
sections.q: Why schedule critical jobs in UTC?
sections.p: How can daylight saving cause a job to skip or repeat?

sections.t: A job that fails silently is worse than one that fails loudly. Send a heartbeat after each success and alert when it goes missing.
sections.q: How can we detect a scheduled job that stopped running?
sections.p: What alerts us when a cron job fails without any error?

sections.t: The app redirects the user to the provider, which returns a short-lived code to the app's callback. The server exchanges that code for tokens over a back channel.
sections.q: How does the authorization code flow deliver tokens to the app?
sections.p: What does the provider send to the callback, and what happens to it afterward?

sections.t: The app generates a random state value before redirecting and checks it on return. A mismatch means the response did not come from the login the app started.
sections.q: What is the state parameter for in OAuth login?
sections.p: How does the app detect a forged callback request?

sections.t: A scope names a permission the app requests, such as reading the profile. Ask only for the scopes the feature needs so users grant less.
sections.q: What does an OAuth scope describe?
sections.p: Why should an app request the narrowest set of permissions?

sections.t: An access token expires quickly, while a refresh token obtains new ones. Store refresh tokens server-side because a stolen one grants long-lived access.
sections.q: What is a refresh token used for?
sections.p: How does an app keep a user signed in after the access token expires?

sections.t: A producer puts a message on the queue and moves on. Consumers process it later, so a slow consumer does not block the producer.
sections.q: How does a queue decouple producers from consumers?
sections.p: Why does a slow consumer not hold up the service that sent the message?

sections.t: A consumer acknowledges a message only after finishing the work. If it crashes first, the broker redelivers the message to another consumer.
sections.q: When should a consumer acknowledge a message?
sections.p: What makes the broker redeliver a message after a consumer crash?

sections.t: A message that fails repeatedly moves to a dead-letter queue after a retry limit. Engineers inspect it there instead of letting it block the main queue.
sections.q: What is a dead-letter queue for?
sections.p: Where do messages go after exhausting their retries?

sections.t: Brokers usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, so a message may arrive twice. Make handlers idempotent by recording processed message ids.
sections.q: Why must queue handlers tolerate duplicate messages?
sections.p: How can a handler safely process a message that arrives twice?
